prompt:
You read a Twitter/X thread by Marius Hobbhahn (unrolled). Extract research choices and the reasoning he gives, as well as any views on how to do research.

Return 3-15 items. Each item is one of:
- "decision": a research decision he (or his team) made, where another choice was possible;
- "rejected": an option, method or line of work he rejected or argued against;
- "disagreement": a place where he disagrees with a default view or practice in the field;
- "advice": advice he gives about how to do research (what to work on, how to test, how to interpret results).
Prefer research methodology (evaluation design, experimental controls, what evidence to trust, which questions to pursue, how strongly to state claims) over biography, logistics or summaries of results. Only include items the text itself supports; return {"decisions": []} if there are none. For each item give:
- item_type: decision / rejected / disagreement / advice
- point: one of D1-D6 (D1 which experiment or hypothesis to pursue; D2 what evidence to collect; D3 whether to accept a result; D4 whether to continue or drop a line of work; D5 how to interpret an ambiguous result; D6 how strongly to state a claim)
- problem: the research problem or question faced, stated neutrally (1 sentence)
- did: what he chose, did or recommends (1 sentence)
- alternatives_named: a JSON list of strings, the alternatives the text itself names or rejects ([] if none)
- stated_reason: the reason the text gives ("" if none)
- quote: a VERBATIM passage of HIS OWN words, 15-60 words, copied character for character, that shows the item. Do not paraphrase, fix spelling or punctuation, merge passages, or use ellipses.
- off_topic: true if the item is not about AI, ML or research practice (e.g. energy policy, health, productivity), else false

Return only JSON: {"decisions": [{"item_type": ..., "point": ..., "problem": ..., "did": ..., "alternatives_named": [...], "stated_reason": ..., "quote": ..., "off_topic": ...}]}

 My Authors

 We modeled the performance of FET-based GPUs assuming that transistor miniaturization will hit a limit before reaching the size of a silicon atom. Our model predicts that performance will plateau between 2027 and 2035 at ~1e14 to 1e15 FLOP/s in FP32. 1/n

epochai.org/blog/predictin… 

 We built a composite model to predict FLOP/s of GPUs from their features. We started with >20 features but found that 2 features (the number of cores and the size of transistors) explain 95% of the variance in historical data. 2/n 

 We first predict a distribution over the limit of miniaturization. The relevant literature suggests that the limit lies somewhere between 3.0nm and 0.7nm. For context, current transistors are ~6nm and the size of a silicon atom is ~0.5nm. 3/n 

 Secondly, we assume that once transistor miniaturization hits its limit GPU producers will still try to leverage additional parallelism by adding additional cores, though this too has a limit. 4/n

 Since each core needs a certain amount of transistors, the approach of building massively-multi-core GPUs will run out of steam a few years after lithographic scaling comes to a halt. 5/n 

 Our model suggests that the top GPU performance will plateau somewhere between 1e14 and 1e15 FLOP/s. This is roughly 2 to 20x the current performance of current state-of-the-art GPUs for FP32. 6/n 

 Our model makes a lot of simplifying assumptions and we expect some clever ways to increase performance, such as 3D chip stacking, as well as architectural improvements. However, we think that limits to miniaturization will pose a significant hurdle for hardware producers. 7/n

 If you have suggestions or feedback, feel free to reach out. 8/n

 This work was done at @epochai under the supervision of @tamaybes. We are very thankful for discussions, feedback and other support from Epoch throughout the entire project. n/n
